tldr: By combining a flow-matching planner trained on 100 hours of VR mocap data with a perceptive whole-body tracker, a humanoid robot navigates cluttered obstacles—stepping over, ducking under, and sidestepping—fully onboard without skill annotations or prebuilt maps.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed PASSAGE system. Starting from 100 hours of scene-aligned motion collected in VR, it integrates a 3-layer elevation map from onboard LiDAR, a 6.25 Hz reference motion planner based on Flow Matching, and a 50 Hz whole-body tracker with geometric feedback (ScaleBFM), operating fully autonomously on a physical Jetson AGX Orin.
overview:
The greatest strength of legged humanoid robots is their ability to flexibly navigate challenging terrain by leveraging their full body of joints. They can step over low hurdles, squeeze sideways through narrow gaps, and duck under low-hanging beams. However, conventional reinforcement learning approaches often require training task-specific policies for each obstacle type and distilling them, or tuning complex reward functions. This makes it difficult to acquire a diverse behavioral repertoire in a unified way. Stitched-together handcrafted motion libraries also face strict limits in adapting to surrounding geometries.

To tackle this, the authors developed PASSAGE, a framework that collects large-scale "Scene-Aligned Demonstrations" matching human movements to surrounding 3D space, and adapts them to unseen obstacle layouts using generative models. Combining a VR headset with inertial motion capture, they gathered 100 hours of traversal motions across 1,500 cluttered procedural scenes. From this data, they built a Flow Matching planner that generates short-horizon reference motion trajectories conditioned on a local destination and a 3-layer geometric elevation map, alongside a whole-body tracker that faithfully follows these trajectories with geometric feedback.

Through simulation and real-world experiments on a Unitree G1, they confirmed a scaling law: expanding captured data from 6 to 100 hours substantially increases contact-free traversal success. Furthermore, by generating local maps online from onboard LiDAR point clouds, the robot traversed 50 unseen physical layouts without prebuilt maps, running entirely on an onboard Jetson AGX Orin.
contributions: Built a 100-hour, 1,500-scene dataset of scene-aligned human traversal using VR and inertial mocap, scaling it to approximately 1,000 hours of effective training pairs via validated scene augmentation.

Decoupled a 6.25 Hz Flow Matching motion planner from a 50 Hz perceptive whole-body tracker with geometric feedback, enabling autonomous selection and composition of diverse traversal behaviors without skill annotations.
Introduced Real-Time Chunking (RTC) and planner-side reinforcement learning post-training under a frozen tracker, drastically improving inter-chunk consistency and closed-loop control stability.
Rigorously demonstrated a scaling effect where increasing training data (from 6 to 100 hours) directly improves closed-loop collision avoidance and traversal success rates.

Realized an end-to-end onboard pipeline on a single Jetson AGX Orin—from onboard LiDAR local occupancy mapping to planning and whole-body control—achieving traversal across 50 unseen real-world layouts.

sections.heading: Can a humanoid navigate cluttered spaces using whole-body motions?
sections.summary: To navigate cluttered obstacles, a humanoid must perceive environmental geometry through onboard sensors and coordinate whole-body motions. This paper proposes PASSAGE, an integrated traversal system that combines 100 hours of scene-aligned motion data, a Flow Matching planner, and a perceptive tracker without relying on skill labels.
sections.details:
Humanoid robots can leverage their human-like degrees of freedom to move sideways through tight openings, stride over low obstacles, and duck beneath overhead barriers. However, autonomously making these decisions from onboard perception and executing them while compensating for errors is far from easy.

Many existing approaches rely on reinforcement learning (RL), such as training expert policies for individual scenes and distilling them (e.g., CAT). Yet, these demand massive computational resources and often restrict whole-body coordination, such as controlling only the 12 lower-body joints. Conversely, motion-matching approaches provide rich whole-body movement priors, but traversing cluttered spaces requires large-scale demonstration data strictly synchronized with the surrounding geometry.

To overcome these hurdles, this work proposes large-scale collection of scene-aligned demonstrations paired with a loosely coupled generative planner-tracker architecture. Built on 100 hours of VR-guided mocap across 1,500 scenes, it links a 6.25 Hz Flow Matching planner with a 50 Hz geometry-aware tracker (ScaleBFM). This allows the robot to select and compose diverse traversal behaviors adapted to unseen geometries without any skill labels or obstacle-specific policies.

sections.heading: Bridging whole-body tracking control and scene-aligned motion generation
sections.summary: While general whole-body trackers following diverse motions with a single policy and terrain-aware locomotion have advanced, generating motion trajectories that satisfy future geometric constraints remains an active pursuit. This work introduces a new pipeline that generates destination-conditioned motions from large-scale environment-coupled demonstrations and executes them with a fixed perceptive tracker.
sections.details:
Humanoid locomotion and motor control have largely evolved along two paths: Whole-Body Control and Scene-Aligned Motion Generation.

### Whole-Body Control and Perceptive Locomotion
Since DeepMimic, general-purpose trackers that follow diverse reference motions via a single RL policy have been widely studied. Extensions such as Perceptive BFM incorporating vision or elevation maps, as well as locomotion skill distillation, have also emerged. However, most existing methods still rely on single-task rewards in simulation or switch between a small, curated library of skills (such as running or jumping), rather than generating whole-body trajectories suited to cluttered spaces in real time.

### Scene-Aligned Data and Generative Models
Recently, efforts have emerged to capture surrounding geometry and human motion simultaneously using cameras or wearable sensors to generate environment-adapted motions. Yet existing datasets have been modest, typically around 2.3 hours across 145 scenes. Furthermore, methods incorporating generative models like diffusion into navigation often require co-training the planner and tracker or adapting the generator to the tracker through complex procedures. PASSAGE stands out by building a 100-hour dataset, cleanly coupling a Flow Matching planner with an independently trained general-purpose perceptive tracker, and fine-tuning only the planner via RL while keeping the tracker frozen.

sections.heading: Forging a planner and tracker from 100 hours of human motion data
sections.summary: The framework consists of 100 hours of motion data gathered in VR, a Flow Matching planner taking a 3-layer elevation map as input, and a geometry-augmented ScaleBFM tracker operating at 50 Hz. High tracking fidelity and safety are achieved using RTC to maintain inter-chunk continuity and planner RL under a frozen tracker.
sections.details:
The design philosophy behind PASSAGE is to decouple geometry-aware motion generation from fast dynamic execution.

### III-A Large-Scale Scene-Aligned Demonstrations
First, 1,500 cluttered procedural environments were created within a 10 m corridor by randomly sampling eight difficulty parameters, such as step width, obstacle height and width, and ceiling/floor presence. An operator wearing a Noitom inertial mocap suit and a VR headset navigated the corridor from a first-person virtual avatar perspective. Virtual collisions were fed back to the operator via haptics, and trials with collisions were automatically discarded. The collected data was retargeted to the 29-DoF Unitree G1, yielding 100 hours (19,310 sequences) of high-quality data. Furthermore, validated scene augmentation—altering obstacle scale and rotation with MuJoCo collision checks—expanded the effective training data to roughly 1,000 hours.

### III-B Modular Planner-Tracker Structure
The planner takes the past 4 frames of motion history, the local goal coordinates, and a body-centric 3-layer elevation map (top occupied surface, underside of overhead clearance, and floor surface) as input. Using Flow Matching, it generates a 25-frame (0.5 s) reference trajectory. Auxiliary losses penalize foot slipping and jerk, while a HumanoidPF potential field loss encourages obstacle repulsion.
For tracking, the authors adopted ScaleBFM, a general-purpose whole-body tracker. By appending 8 CNN-encoded terrain tokens to the proprioceptive tokens and further training with PPO, the tracker learns micro-adjustments around nearby walls even in confined spaces.

### III-C Planner Refinement: RTC and Frozen-Tracker RL
Re-planning with a generative model at fixed intervals (6.25 Hz) often leads to discontinuities at chunk boundaries. To address this, Soft RTC (Real-Time Chunking) blends the tail of the previous plan smoothly into the new one. In addition, with the trained tracker completely fixed (frozen), the planner undergoes RL post-training (PPO adapted from ReinFlow) where the robot executes the generated trajectories and receives rewards for reaching the destination and avoiding collisions. This guides the planner to naturally generate trajectories that are physically trackable by the robot.

captions.F3: Scene-aligned motion capture setup using VR. An operator wearing an inertial suit and VR headset navigates virtual obstacle courses in first-person view (inset), collecting natural human motions that align perfectly with the surrounding geometry by walking, stepping over, and ducking under barriers.

sections.heading: Data scaling unlocks traversal leaps and tackles 50 physical layouts
sections.summary: In simulation, scaling the captured data from 6 to 100 hours improved the contact-free success rate from 48.1% to 68.9%. In real-world experiments on a Unitree G1, the fully onboard system traversed all 50 unseen physical obstacle layouts without falling, achieving completely contact-free traversal in 90% of trials.
sections.details:
The experiments thoroughly validate whether the proposed method can autonomously select diverse whole-body traversal behaviors and how scaling data volume impacts closed-loop performance.

### IV-A & IV-B Evaluation Setup and Benchmark Comparisons
Evaluation was performed in MuJoCo across 150 unseen test environments spanning three difficulty levels (750 episodes). Baseline comparisons included CAT, a representative RL-based method, and a diffusion-based pipeline (Zhang et al. style) implemented under equivalent conditions.
PASSAGE's final model achieved a 98.7% success rate and a 70.3% contact-free success rate (CF-Succ.). In contrast, CAT achieved 70.3% success with only 14.0% contact-free, and the Zhang et al. style pipeline on 12 hours of data achieved 86.0% success with 19.2% contact-free. This highlights PASSAGE's ability to produce safe, collision-averse motions (even on 12 hours of data, PASSAGE reached 48.6% contact-free success).

### IV-C Data Scaling Laws
Performance was measured across three independent seeds as data scaled from 6h to 12h, 24h, 48h, and 100h. Goal success increased monotonically from 84.3% to 96.4%, contact-free success jumped from 48.1% to 68.9%, and contact duration per distance plummeted from 0.3565 s/m to 0.0499 s/m. With scene augmentation (equivalent to 1,000h), contact-free success reached 70.3%, showing that high-quality scene-aligned data volume is the key to generalization.

### IV-D Ablation Studies
Ablations confirmed the importance of each component. Removing RTC caused contact-free success to plummet from 70.3% to 24.5%, proving that chunk boundary discontinuities directly cause collisions. Removing frozen-tracker RL dropped contact-free success to 26.4%, while removing perceptive augmentation from the tracker spiked the fall rate from 0.9% to 6.9%. Every piece plays a vital role.

### IV-E Onboard Real-World Evaluation
On the physical Unitree G1, experiments were conducted across 50 unseen physical layouts constructed from cardboard boxes and foam blocks. In demanding configurations involving stepping over, ducking under, sidestepping, and even climbing over a fallen robot, the system reached the goal without falls or emergency stops in all 50 trials, clearing 45 trials (90%) completely free of obstacle contact.

captions.F6: Representative traversal behaviors in simulation and real-world experiments. A single model autonomously selects and composes diverse behaviors: ducking under overhead obstacles (a), stepping over low barriers (b), ducking immediately after stepping over (c), crab-walking through narrow gaps (f), and stepping over a fallen robot (h).

sections.heading: Conclusions and what lies ahead
sections.summary: PASSAGE substantially elevates humanoid whole-body traversal by pairing large-scale scene-aligned demonstration data with a generative planner and a perceptive tracker. Future work points toward parkour behaviors with steep elevation changes, such as stairs or vaults, and integrating RGB cameras to detect thin wires.
sections.details:
This paper presented PASSAGE, a framework for goal-directed humanoid traversal in cluttered spaces. By coherently integrating 100 hours of VR-guided mocap collection, Flow Matching motion planning, geometry-augmented ScaleBFM tracking, and fully onboard deployment, the authors demonstrated that a robot can autonomously select whole-body behaviors without individual skill labels.

Demonstrating that data scaling steadily improves collision avoidance, alongside executing LiDAR SLAM, planning (6.25 Hz), and control (50 Hz) entirely on an onboard Jetson AGX Orin, represents a major milestone toward practical deployment.

Future directions include expanding the behavioral repertoire to more acrobatic movements with large vertical changes, such as climbing stairs, leaping onto elevated platforms, and vaulting obstacles. Additionally, integrating visual inputs such as RGB cameras into the geometric representation will help detect thin cables or transparent glass that remain difficult for LiDAR alone to capture.

sections.heading: Appendix: 3-layer elevation map extraction and onboard implementation details
sections.summary: A closer look at the 3-layer elevation mapping algorithm, the Flow Matching network structure, and multiprocess pipelining on the Jetson AGX Orin that power real-world deployment.
sections.details:
### Real-Time 3-Layer Elevation Mapping
At the core of this approach is a 3-layer elevation map that compactly represents vertical spatial structures. LiDAR point clouds and odometry from the robot are integrated into a voxel grid via ROG-Map. For each vertical voxel column, the algorithm extracts: (1) the highest occupied voxel (floor surface or obstacle top), (2) the top of known free space beneath it (obstacle underside), and (3) the support surface below (the floor the robot can step on). If duckable clearance exists overhead, all three heights are recorded; where no clearance exists, a single height is duplicated across channels. Unobserved space is never treated as free space, ensuring a fail-safe design.

### Onboard Planner and Tracker Implementation
On the Jetson AGX Orin, the planner model is converted from ONNX into TensorRT FP16. The planner runs as an independent process at 6.25 Hz (160 ms period) and communicates with the 50 Hz C++ control thread via multiprocessing pipes and POSIX shared memory. Target joint positions produced by the tracker are forwarded to the robot's low-level motor controllers at 500 Hz. This multi-rate loop enables real-time whole-body obstacle avoidance without relying on offboard computation.

captions.F4: Comparison of 3-layer geometric elevation maps in simulation (left) and from the onboard physical LiDAR (right). The top, middle, and bottom layers accurately capture not only the floor surface for foot placement, but also the underside of overhead beams to duck beneath and the tops of obstacles to step over.

takeaways: Scaling scene-aligned demonstration data where environment geometry matches motion monotonically improves closed-loop collision avoidance and traversal success in humanoid robots.
Decoupling coarse motion planning via generative models (Flow Matching) from an RL tracker with local geometric feedback is highly stable and scalable for whole-body control.
Soft RTC for chunk boundary continuity and planner RL (ReinFlow) under a frozen tracker are crucial for ensuring real-world smoothness and collision-free safety.
Compressing complex 3D geometry into a 3-layer elevation map allows onboard LiDAR to reliably and efficiently capture both overhead clearance and floor surfaces.
limitations: The current behavioral repertoire is limited to ground-level obstacle traversal (stepping over, ducking under, squeezing past) and does not support large vertical changes such as stairs or high jumps.
Because perception relies on 3D LiDAR geometry, detecting transparent glass panels, thin wires, or hanging ropes remains difficult.
In real-world experiments, contact occurred in 10% of trials (5 out of 50), indicating residual contact risks from tracking errors in millimeter-tight clearances.
